summary:
What we developed: a public web calendar of satellite hotspots for a chosen land area, every month from July 2002 to now, coloured on one consistent scale. It holds real Aqua MODIS counts through December 2021 and, from January 2022, VIIRS counts converted to Aqua-equivalent by one frozen method, C1. The switch between instruments is drawn as a ruled line, not hidden, and the record refreshes daily from NASA FIRMS near-real-time data. Each month names the satellites that fed it, an anomaly view compares it with a reference period, and both the counts and the hotspots download as CSV.

How it addresses the challenge: MODIS and VIIRS detect hotspots differently, so a record that simply joins them does not read on one scale across the change. C1 converts VIIRS counts into Aqua MODIS units. It was chosen by a rule fixed before scoring and tested on held-back years against named baselines; where it passed and where it failed is stated on the site's evidence page.

Why it matters: comparing this month with the same months of past years is the basic question for monitoring burning, and it is only meaningful on one scale. The calendar answers it at one public link, with no login, for seven evaluated regions.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

A public web calendar of satellite hotspots. For a chosen land area it draws a year-by-month grid from July 2002 to now, each month coloured by its hotspot count on one scale. Through December 2021 the counts are real Aqua MODIS; from January 2022 they are VIIRS counts converted to Aqua-equivalent by one frozen method, C1. The switch is drawn as a ruled line on the grid. Months outside the record are hatched so they never look like zero, and incomplete or near-real-time months are marked. Hovering or tapping a month shows its exact count and the satellites that fed it.

Around the calendar: a current-month card that sets this month so far against the same days of every past year; an anomaly view against a reference period the reader can change; the raw splice (MODIS then VIIRS with no conversion) to see the step the record avoids; the typical season and this year's running total; a map of one month's hotspots; a Mann-Kendall trend test with a caution about the sensor switch; two areas side by side; and a globe of 1° cells flagged as unusual. An evidence page shows every scored method, and an about page explains the data and its limits. Counts and hotspots download as CSV.

HOW IT WORKS

A pipeline downloads hotspots per satellite from NASA FIRMS, standard and near-real-time, and refreshes daily. Offshore rows and static heat sources are marked, not deleted. From 2022 each VIIRS hotspot is weighted by C1, so a month's weights add up to an Aqua-equivalent count. C1 blends a transfer table of Aqua-to-VIIRS ratios per calendar month, by day and by night, with a per-footprint model that estimates the chance Aqua would have detected each VIIRS hotspot from its radiative power and viewing angle. Its parameters were fitted on tuning years and frozen, and the product's code reproduces the scored predictions within 1e-6. The pipeline grids the record at 1° and 0.25°, computes the statistics and anomaly flags, and publishes a versioned store. A read-only service answers the web app; every number is computed once on the server, and the browser computes none.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Comparing this month with the same months of past years only means something on one scale, and today FIRMS serves each sensor as it is, with no harmonized monthly record. This project gives scientists who study burning, monitoring agencies and land managers that record at one public link with no login, with its sources and limits shown beside the numbers.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

Instead of hiding the instrument change, the calendar draws it, and the reader can switch to the raw splice to see the step. The method was chosen by a rule fixed before any scores were seen, and the results are reported as they came out, including where C1 failed:

- C1 has 27.9% lower count error than one global factor, baseline (b), on the final set, 95% interval 18.6% to 30.5%, beyond noise. It also passed against the raw splice, baseline (a). Baseline (c), Aqua only, is not scored on count error.

- C1 failed the flag-precision test against (b): 0.704 against 0.736. Under the rule fixed beforehand the outcome was "nothing beat one global factor", and the project lead kept C1 as a recorded deviation after seeing the scores.

- The trade-off: on the final set C1's flags caught more of the true anomalies than (b)'s (recall 0.761 against 0.690) and were right less often. In plain words, more true alerts and more false alarms.

- The final-set score is slightly optimistic because C1 is the best of three.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Missing is not zero: months with no data show as missing, never as 0.

- Fixed claims: every result sentence is written once and checked against the score files.

- Where it is weaker: On the final set, flags in southern Africa were right less than half the time for every candidate method and both baselines: C1 0.453, 4A 0.473, 1A 0.408, (b) 0.459, (a) 0.164. NOAA-20 is untested against Aqua. The comparison of NOAA-20 with Suomi NPP is reported only.

- What the record cannot show: it holds hotspot counts over land only, with no smoke, haze, air quality or burned area, and cloud, thick smoke and smouldering peat can hide burning from the satellites.

- Accessibility: it works by keyboard and at phone width, and its marks do not rely on colour.

- Open and reproducible: the code is public, and secrets are kept out of the repository and scanned for.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

Python 3.14 (uv, FastAPI, DuckDB, PyArrow, Shapely, NumPy, pandas) for the pipeline and the service; React, TypeScript, Vite, D3 and MapLibre GL for the web app; pytest, Vitest and Playwright for tests; GitHub Actions for the daily refresh; a Hugging Face dataset for the build data; Vercel hosts the web app and the service.
